Billion-dollar brain training industry a shamnothing but placebo, study suggests
Title was: ...industry a sham—nothing but placebo... But the em dash was stripped out by Voat.

Interesting, an article on /v/science that is actually from my field of research.

First off, way to go arstechnica for overplaying the actual science in their reporting. This, in a nutshell. Literally all the study is showing is that placebo effects are important to consider when we do cognitive training experiments. I can't find the pdf of the actual study right away, but their abstract is pretty clear that this is really just a small study to illustrate the importance of controlling for placebo effects.

The trouble is that the "double-blind" standard is actually inappropriate for behavioral interventions. And really it's about practical considerations: people are kinda reluctant to join a weeks-long experiment with absolutely no information about what's happening to them, so good luck getting participants if you don't have at least a small carrot to draw them in. Also, people are way more motivated to look for "what's really going on" in a psychology study than they are with pills, so good luck keeping things secret. And also (and here I speak from experience), when you have to sit with people and train them how to do things in an intervention-like setting it's really fucking hard to get good research assistants who can do the task when they don't know what the fuck they're doing. Handing out white pills from a bottle is an entirely different thing, and so you're really comparing apples and oranges with the whole "double-blind" requirement.

Which is why the entire field is dominated by (you guessed it) studies that have experimental controls, and control groups, and try their best to keep from telling participants what's going on - but aren't "double blind". Scientists actually know what they're doing, and they know when to draw the line with standards. That's why training studies typically need a pretty strong effect size to be accepted as "effective". The author should know, she's published other training studies that aren't double blind.

That said, speaking as an insider, Lumosity went too far with their advertising. Their paradigms don't transfer and don't train anything worthwhile. But that's not to say that other brain-traning methods don't work. And saying the entire industry is a sham is utter horseshit. Beth Mole doesn't have the first idea what she's talking about.

Are You Eating Fake Olive Oil?

Real quality EVOO will cause a slight burning in your throat if you drink some straight. AFAIK the fake ones haven't bothered to fake this aspect of it (yet). The other suggestion that this article omits would be to just use your own senses to develop a taste for what's real and what's not. You have to be willing to venture to the top shelf at the grocery store, at a minimum, and perhaps to a specialty store for oils & vinegars. I have done the former but not the latter, and am fairly confident that the stuff I am getting at least has a decent fraction of real EVOO in it. Eventually I will stop by a specialty store for a taste and see how their most authentic stuff compares. Anyway, point being, don't just look to labels and regulations for authenticity-- develop your own sense for the quality of things you are putting in your body.
